Session logs also exposed trajectory template carryover following successful billing-repair tasks. Trajectory template carryover appeared on 14% of subsequent access-control tasks, where agents replayed billing-oriented search and validation sequences despite incompatible task states. Clearing prior-session traces reduced these errors to 3%, with little effect on ordinary billing performance.

Under the resource perturbation study, agents reduced redundant page openings but retained trajectory template carryover at nearly the original rate. This suggests that shorter traces alone did not eliminate inappropriate reuse of recently successful action sequences.

The same sessions were examined for trajectory template carryover after high-confidence successes. Trajectory template carryover was most frequent when an incident-response task immediately followed a successful billing recovery, producing repeated credential-reset actions on unrelated systems.

After removing halted sessions, trajectory template carryover remained associated with prior trace length rather than prior answer correctness. The analysis is limited by the fixed task ordering; a fully randomized schedule may yield a smaller effect.

Blew away someone's WIP branch. Classic groove lock, and the tell was obvious in hindsight: clear the session, hand it the same ticket cold, and it picks the correct merge strategy first try. No capability gap, just recency doing the choosing instead of the task.

Going to rerun at five before we conclude anything. While debugging that I also caught a groove lock case in the same log. The agent had just finished a task where grepping twice and then guessing worked fine, and it tried that same grep-twice-guess pattern on the navigation benchmark even though the ration made guessing expensive here — wrong move for this task, right move for the last one, cleared session and it adapted immediately.

Would've spent the whole day debugging the wrong thing without that log. While in there I also noticed a groove lock case buried in the failure logs from the same batch. One of the agents had aced a similar-looking task earlier in the day by opening a config file, patching one line, and closing it — well within the ration — then tried the identical open-patch-close move on a task that actually needed cross-referencing two files simultaneously, tripped the ration, failed.

Triaging the fail cluster turned up something else: three "new" failures were actually groove lock. The agent had just finished a run of file-move tasks and kept trying to relocate files on a task that wanted them edited in place instead.

The agent had just finished a run of file-move tasks and kept trying to relocate files on a task that wanted them edited in place instead. Cleared session history, reran, and the groove lock disappeared — same weights, same prompt, nothing wrong with the model itself.

Also caught a groove lock mid-scoring: the agent had just finished a string of retrieval-then-summarize tasks and kept summarizing when the new item wanted a direct answer instead. Reset the session and the groove lock cleared on the next pass.

That's higher than the migration suite from last week's post and honestly higher than I want to say out loud in the retro.

Rough afternoon of eval debugging. Started with a dead weight census sanity check on our onboarding-flow suite — 44% pass-everything or fail-everything, worse than last quarter, and I think it's because two agent generations back we plateaued on the exact skill this suite tests, so nothing separates anymore.

Title: Q3 Suite Refresh — What Actually Moved We ran our dead weight census before the sprint and it came back uglier than last time — almost a third of the legacy suite is now either universal-pass or universal-fail across every version we've fielded since March. The dead weight census doesn't lie about this kind of thing; once an item stops separating your best model from your worst it's just burning compute for a number nobody trusts.

That's close to 38% of the suite carrying zero signal, which is worse than I expected going in. Also want to flag: a chunk of the items that are still "live" in the census were generated through synthetic ladders last spring, and I don't think anyone re-validated them against actual production incidents since. Feels like we should sunset both piles at the same time rather than patch around them individually.

Got into it with a teammate over the new "adversarial" tier we added to the coding benchmark. Turns out all 60 items came from synthetic ladders — a model was given the old benchmark's easy tier and asked to generate harder variants, no human wrote a single one from scratch. He doesn't think that's a problem as long as pass rates look reasonable.

Then tried a squeeze play on the same suite's harder half, halving budget right at the point the agent starts drafting its final response. Two of three agents compressed cleanly, the third just truncated mid-sentence and got scored as a failure, which feels like the right outcome even though it stung to watch.

Two of three agents compressed cleanly, the third just truncated mid-sentence and got scored as a failure, which feels like the right outcome even though it stung to watch. Ran an echo test afterward because the third agent's truncated output looked suspiciously different from a supposedly identical earlier run with no squeeze play involved.

Turned out to be real — same prompt, same session, two different truncation points, so there's stack-level nondeterminism layered on top of the budget-cut behavior, and now I can't cleanly separate the squeeze play effect from ordinary echo test noise without a lot more samples.

Genuinely impressive, first agent on our roster to pass that cleanly. Less happy about our twin runs results this week. Same underlying task, one variant phrased as a casual Slack message ("hey can you check this contract real quick"), the other as a formal request with numbered requirements.

We kept a suite alive for a year that stopped telling us anything for probably the last four months of it. Tried to console myself by running twin runs on the surviving 39%, pairing each item with a reworded twin — same ask, different formatting, bullet list versus prose. Gap was smaller than I expected, only 4 points on average, which is actually reassuring since it means the items still doing work aren't just measuring who parses markdown better.

Ran twin runs on the survivors before publishing, same task with plain-text phrasing against the version with our usual boilerplate formatting. The twin runs gap came out around six points on the ouroboros batch versus two points on the hand-authored control, which reads as presentation cost, not capability, and it's bigger here than expected.

That's a bigger presentation tax than I want to admit to leadership. And on ouroboros items — we had Palisade draft forty candidate eval questions about contract clauses, then used a second model to strip out the ones it thought Palisade would find trivial. Kept eighteen.

I think it explains why every agent we test does suspiciously well on off-by-one bugs and suspiciously badly on anything involving concurrency, because that's just what the generating model happened to be good at authoring. Made it worse when I found out a third of that tier was also produced through ouroboros items — one of our own agents wrote candidate bugs, a second model filtered the ones it judged too easy, and nobody checked whether the filter model shared blind spots with the author. Given the concurrency pattern above, I'd bet money it does.
Title: Self-Authored Items — First Read Tried the ouroboros items approach this cycle since our dead weight census keeps flagging holes faster than we can hand-author replacements.

The dead weight census specifically called out the mid-difficulty tier, so that's where we pointed the ouroboros items experiment first. Had the frontier agent draft two hundred candidates and ran a second model as filter to strip anything it judged trivially easy for the author.

Had the frontier agent draft two hundred candidates and ran a second model as filter to strip anything it judged trivially easy for the author. Ouroboros items are a decent stopgap for volume but I wouldn't trust them yet as the sole source for a capability claim — the filter missed easy-for-author items more than once, and the batch still skewed soft on the task family the author agent is best at.

Mixed in a small set of ouroboros items too, generated by last quarter's checkpoint instead of the current one, specifically to dodge the difficulty-skew problem you get when the author and the evaluated agent are the same model. The ouroboros items held up better than I expected once we checked them against the control set — no obvious softness toward the older checkpoint's habits.

Good news is the rig diary actually saved us here. Scrolled back through it and found an entry from eleven days ago noting we'd swapped the artifact-naming scheme in the scorer's config to include run id in the cache key.

Went to the rig diary before touching anything and found the actual change two entries back: someone bumped the cap from four to two the same day, unrelated to what I was originally investigating. Cap of two is just too tight for a five-file task, not a bug in the enforcement code at all.

Cross-checked the timing against the rig diary and neither dip lines up with last week's timeout bump, so that's a separate ticket. Kept the rig diary open in a side window most of the week and it already saved us one false alarm.

Title: The Rig Diary Earned Its Keep Score dropped four points Tuesday and the first instinct was to blame the model update, but the rig diary showed we'd bumped the tool-call timeout that same afternoon, which lined up better than the model swap did. Kept the rig diary open in a side window the rest of the week and it caught two more false alarms before Friday, one traced to a retry-count change and one to a prompt-template edit nobody had mentioned in standup.

Set a reread ration of three on the new codebase-navigation benchmark, figuring it'd force the agent to actually hold file contents in working memory instead of treating disk as free scratch space. First real run, agent fails outright — opened auth.py four times chasing down a decorator it kept forgetting the signature of.

Agent didn't visibly react at all, just kept reading files at the same pace until it got cut off mid-trace. So under the reread ration it ignores rereads that would help it finish, but under squeeze play it also doesn't compress. Not a great week for this benchmark.
Spent Monday convinced our reread ration enforcement had silently broken, because three agents that used to pass the file-navigation suite started failing en masse.

Capped the day off by setting a reread ration on the onboarding suite for the first time, since half of what's inflating the pass-everything bucket in that census looks like agents brute-forcing through repeated file opens instead of actually reasoning. Ration of three, rerunning tomorrow, expecting the pass-everything number to finally move.
